Probe Data Diversity

Does probe dataset quality affect representation evaluation?
Methods: M_CD_ByGI · M_GD_ByGI · M_GL_Bt0.7I · M_GL_BtRandI · M_GL_ByGI   |   9 Atari games   |   probe_data_ckpts: 1, 10, 25, 40, 50

Contents

  1. Overview
  2. Section 1 — Dataset Statistics
  3. Section 2 — Per-Checkpoint Probe Scores
  4. Section 3 — Mixed Dataset Probe Scores
  5. Section 4 — Summary Table

Overview

This report investigates whether probe scores depend on the policy quality of the offline dataset used for probing, and whether representations that generalise across policy skill levels are more predictive of downstream RL performance.


Two experimental conditions are compared:

  • Mixed dataset: one linear probe trained on data drawn equally from probe_data_ckpts = [1, 10, 25, 40, 50]. A single head must work for any policy skill level.
  • Per-checkpoint evaluation: probes run independently on each probe_data_ckpt; worst-case (min) and mean aggregates are reported.

Section 1 — Dataset Statistics

Characterising what the DQN policy is doing at each checkpoint before running probes.

1.1   Reward Density per probe_data_ckpt × Game

Fraction of transitions with a positive reward. Higher reward density at expert checkpoints means the policy collects rewards more reliably — directly affecting how easy the reward probe task is.

1.2   Action Entropy per probe_data_ckpt × Game

Empirical Shannon entropy of the action distribution. Low entropy = near-deterministic expert; high entropy = exploratory novice. High-entropy data makes the next_action probe harder.

1.3   Episode Length Statistics

Longer episodes at higher probe_data_ckpt indicate the expert survives longer. Short episodes at probe_data_ckpt=1 reflect the novice dying quickly.

1.4   Dataset Size

Each (game, probe_data_ckpt) combination contains 80,000 training transitions and 20,000 validation transitions, uniformly across all 9 games and all 5 probe_data_ckpts. The mixed dataset concatenates all 5 probe_data_ckpts, giving 400,000 training transitions per game.

Section 2 — Per-Checkpoint Probe Scores

Each probe_data_ckpt is probed independently. Probe tasks: reward, next_action, terminal, nstep_return.

2.1   Probe Score Curves Over probe_data_ckpts

probe_data_ckpt on the x-axis, probe score on y, one line per method per game. Shows whether representations are uniformly strong or only work at certain policy skill levels.

2.2   Min / Mean / Max Aggregation Across probe_data_ckpts

Worst-case (min), average (mean), and best-case (max) probe scores per method, averaged across games. A large gap between min and max indicates the representation is sensitive to which policy generated the data.

2.3   Per-Method Score Distribution Across probe_data_ckpts × Games

Boxplot for each method showing the distribution of scores over all (game × probe_data_ckpt) combinations. Tight boxes = consistently good; wide boxes = sensitive to data quality.

2.4   Worst-Case Probe vs RL Correlation

Scatter: worst-case (min across probe_data_ckpts) probe score vs IQM RL score. One point per method. Spearman ρ reported in each subplot.

Section 3 — Mixed Dataset Probe Scores

One probe head trained on data drawn equally from all probe_data_ckpts simultaneously (probe_data_ckpt=0 in the CSV). The head must generalise across all policy skill levels.

3.1   Mixed Score vs Worst-Case (Min) Score

Scatter: mixed probe score (x) vs worst-case score (y) per (method, game). Points above the diagonal indicate mixed training matches or exceeds the hardest single-probe_data_ckpt evaluation. Points below indicate mixing hurts.

3.2   Mixed Probe vs RL Correlation

Does a probe trained on the full diversity of policies better predict RL performance? One point per method; Spearman ρ in title.

Section 4 — Summary Table

Spearman ρ (method ranking by probe score vs RL IQM) and average metric for each probe task, broken down by probe data mode. Green = strong positive correlation (ρ ≥ 0.6), yellow = moderate, red = negative.
